title: Out of the belly (Jonah 2)
hookLine: from inside the fish, Jonah prays

cards: Inside the fish there is no sky, no shore, no way to tell the hour. The text gives the whole thing in one plain sentence.

In the King James words: "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights." A prophet who ran as far as he could has run out of places to go.
And there, of all places, Jonah prays.

teach.h: A PRAYER FROM INSIDE THE FISH.
teach.b: "Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly." And what he says is surprising. It isn't mainly a plea to get out.

It sounds more like a psalm of thanks. "I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice." Belly of hell, in the King James.

teach.h: THE BELLY OF SHEOL, THE BOTTOM OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: The Hebrew word is Sheol, which the 1917 Jewish translation renders the nether-world. Jonah is inside a fish, and he describes it as the bottom of the world. All thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
The weeds were wrapped about my head. I went down to the bottoms of the mountains. Down again, the direction he's gone since Joppa.

teach.h: WHEN MY SOUL FAINTED, I REMEMBERED.
teach.b: Then the prayer turns: "When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD." Notice the tense. He speaks of being heard while still inside.
Some readers find a strange hope in that: thanks before the rescue, from the low place itself. It ends on a short line, "Salvation is of the LORD."
Then, the text says plainly, the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land. No ceremony. Just dry ground under his feet.
The man who kept going down finally calls up, and he does it without waiting to climb out first.

how: Jonah's prayer is read in synagogue as part of the book of Jonah on Yom Kippur afternoon, and its lines echo the language of the Psalms.

o: the port city where Jonah paid his fare and boarded a ship
the depths below, the nether-world in the 1917 translation
the great city that fasted in sackcloth when Jonah warned it

games.q: out of the belly — tap the pairs.

s: Jonah's prayer in the fish is mostly begging to be let out
it reads like a psalm of thanks: he cried, and he was heard.
Jonah speaks of being heard while he's still inside the fish
the thanks come before the rescue.
the prayer ends: salvation is of the LORD
a short line, and then the fish lets him go.

games.q: you're Jonah, inside the fish, in the dark. what do you do?
o: wait silently to see what happens.
games.why: Jonah prays from the fish's belly, and speaks as if already heard: I cried, and thou heardest my voice.

practice: Name, quietly, where you are right now, not where you hope to be: tired, stuck, worried, grieving, or simply fine, and don't wait to feel better before you speak; Jonah didn't.
If you pray, you can use his own words: I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me. If you don't, just say plainly, to yourself, what the low place is like.

wordCard.voice: Sheol. Hebrew for the nether-world: Jonah's prayer from inside the fish, from the low place, before he's out. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: from the belly of Sheol, Jonah 2:3 (KJV 2:2); the 1917 Jewish translation has the nether-world.

carryVoice: Your line: heard before he was out. Thanks, from the low place itself. Day eight hundred twenty-five, done.
